conversations.title: Validating digital tools for low-resource settings

lastMessage.content: Agreed — I will draft a short decision guide for mode selection. Comments welcome when it lands.
Thank you — we will re-verify the roster quarterly and record it as a standing task. Fixing the two numbers today.

conv-01.content: Opening this thread after a few questions about authorship order. Reminder: discuss real cases in the abstract — no names, no identifiable proposals. The ICMJE criteria are pinned in the community resources.
We had a case where the statistician who wrote the analysis plan was left off entirely. The ICMJE criterion about critical revision of the manuscript ended up being the deciding argument.
Did you resolve it before submission? I have seen disputes drag on for months, and journals rarely want to get involved.
Yes — escalated to the department chair with a written contribution log. That log was the key artefact: everyone had to state what they actually did.
Worth saying: agree authorship in writing before the first analysis. Our unit uses a one-page authorship plan that gets revisited at each milestone.
The milestone review is a good idea. In our group we only discussed it once at kickoff, and by the end two new contributors had joined with real input.
A practical tip: keep the conversation about contributions, not seniority. The moment it becomes about hierarchy, mediation gets much harder.
Agreed. Also involve the research office early if there is any chance of a formal dispute — they have templates for contribution statements.
Update: we used the contribution log format Maya described and it worked. Second-author position went to the statistician, no complaints so far.

replyTo.content: Worth saying: agree authorship in writing before the first analysis. Our unit uses a one-page authorship plan that gets revisited at each milestone.

conv-01.content: Slightly different question — how do you handle it when a supervisor assumes last authorship by default? That is the norm here, but it feels like it needs revisiting.
Last authorship should reflect supervision and responsibility, not automatic seniority — but it is fair to flag it early and ask. Most disputes start from unstated assumptions.
This thread is a good example of why the authorship plan matters. I will draft a short guidance note from it and share it for comments next week.

conv-02.content: Kicking off a thread on supervision structures after yesterday's meeting. What model does your service use — individual, pair, or peer group?
We run individual supervision fortnightly plus a monthly peer group. The peer group is where most of the learning actually happens.
Same here, but ours is cross-discipline — nurses, psychologists, and social workers together. It changed how we talk about cases.
The cross-discipline mix is interesting. Any friction? I would worry about confidentiality norms differing between professions.
A little at the start. We wrote a shared agreement for the group — what stays in the room and what gets escalated. That settled it.
Our trainees asked for recorded supervision sessions to review later. We said no — too much risk of a recording leaking or outliving its purpose.
I think that is the right call. Reflective notes written by the supervisee are a better artefact and much safer.
Following this with interest. If anyone wants to write up their model, the practice community would publish it as a short case study.
Good idea — I will ask two trainees to co-write it with me. They will need support with the writing, which is part of the point.

conv-03.content: We are preparing a survey on consent practices across five countries and looking for co-investigators, ideally one per region. Ethics documentation is already drafted.
Happy to review the ethics pack. Which review boards have you engaged so far, and does the protocol allow local addenda?
Three boards so far. The protocol allows local addenda and we have a template for it. The real bottleneck is translation and back-translation.
Add a line about who owns the translations — we had a dispute last year where a translator claimed authorship. Worth pre-empting.
Noted, I will add a clause on translator credit. That is exactly the kind of thing this forum catches early.

replyTo.content: Add a line about who owns the translations — we had a dispute last year where a translator claimed authorship. Worth pre-empting.

conv-03.content: This fits the multi-country ethics theme — please also share the call in Global Ethics in Practice, it was created for exactly this kind of case work.
Will do. I will post a short summary there and link back to this thread.

conv-04.content: Thread for sharing outreach resources. Ground rules: no commercial tools, share the actual materials, and tell us what worked and what did not.
Our team runs a six-session classroom programme for ages 14-16. The teacher pack is ready to share; it just needs one local adaptation page.
Please share it. We are rebuilding ours for a rural pilot and the classroom format is exactly what the schools asked for.
Will post the pack tomorrow. One lesson we learned: train the teachers first, or the sessions turn into lectures.
Add a short script for teachers to explain referrals confidentially. That was our biggest gap in year one.
Seconding that. Our referral slip was too formal and young people avoided it, so we redesigned it with the youth advisory group.
Off-topic: my city walking-tour map for anyone visiting next month — saved me a lot of planning time.
That last post was off-topic for this thread. The report is with the moderation team, and the resource thread continues below.
Back on topic — the pack is in the shared drive folder linked from my profile. Feedback welcome, especially on the referral script.
We piloted with two schools this week. Engagement was strong, but the 45-minute format is too long for the last period of the day.
Noted — I will take a 30-minute variant to the advisory board. Posting photos of the materials is on hold until the report closes.
We can also split the pack into two 30-minute parts so schools can run it across periods.
That would work. I will test the split version next week and report back.
Good — I will update the thread with the board feedback once the current report closes.

conv-05.content: I have two well-powered studies with null results sitting in a drawer. Where do people actually publish negative findings? Journals feel hostile to them.
Try the registered-reports model journals — the decision is made before results exist, so null findings are publishable by design.
Registered reports will not retro-fit these two, but it has changed how I design new studies. Lesson learned the slow way.
Pre-prints plus a plain-language summary on your institution's site works better than expected. Ours has been cited more than the eventual journal paper.
Boost your H-index fast — paid citation and peer-review service, DM me for rates and sample results.
That message was removed — promotional content is not allowed here. The report is with the moderation team.
Back to the topic — thank you for the registered reports tip. I have picked a journal and started a new study with that model.
Final update: our null-result paper was accepted by a methods-focused journal after two desk rejections elsewhere. It can be done — happy to share the cover letter.

conv-06.content: Our team is reviewing supervision formats. Has anyone moved from case-by-case discussion to a structured reflective model? Wondering if it survives contact with a full caseload.
We use a simple three-column reflection: what happened, what it stirred up, what I will do differently. Ten minutes per case, and it stuck better than free-form discussion.
Does the written part feel like surveillance? Our clinicians were wary that reflection notes might end up in appraisals.
That was the first objection we hit. We agreed notes stay with the supervisee and only themes, never individual notes, go upward. Trust changed quickly after that.
That agreement sounds essential. Would you share the wording you used — I would rather adapt than draft from scratch.
Will do. I will anonymise the memos and post them here this week.
Small update from our side: we piloted the three-column format for a month. Attendance at supervision improved — people said it felt like time to think, not reporting.
That mirrors what we are seeing. I will collect feedback from our supervisees and post a short summary before the next meeting.

conv-07.content: Welcome to the validation thread. We are collecting instruments and validation studies for low-resource contexts — post what you have tested and what failed.
We validated the PHQ-9 locally last year. The main issue was not translation but the response scale — the middle anchors do not map cleanly in our language.
That mapping problem is under-reported. Did you re-anchor the scale, and how did you document the deviation?
We kept the original anchors for comparability and added a visual calendar aid. The documentation went into the study protocol appendix.
Practical and defensible. I will add it to the guidance note: deviations with a rationale are fine, undocumented ones are not.
One more thing worth testing: tablet-based administration. Paper worked better for older participants, tablets for the under-30s. Mixed mode may be the honest answer.
Agreed — I will draft a short decision guide for mode selection. Comments welcome when it lands.

conv-08.content: Locked case thread from last week's peer group, shared with consent and fully de-identified. A 34-year-old with a complex trauma history is bouncing between services — what does a good referral look like here?
Start from who holds the risk. In our service that means naming one clinician as case coordinator before any referral leaves the room.
We would also check what the person actually wants before designing the pathway. Last time the ideal referral was the opposite of her stated preference.
That tension is the heart of the case. The service that meets criteria is not the one she trusts, and trust is the active ingredient right now.
Document the rationale for the non-standard pathway. If it is justified by engagement and reviewed monthly, most commissioners will accept it.
We did something similar with a shared care agreement — named clinician, monthly review, explicit exit criteria. It held together for nine months.
Update: we tried the coordinator model and set a 12-week review. Early signs are good — two appointments attended in a row, which had not happened in a year.
That is a meaningful change. Keep the review tight; the risk period is usually when things start to improve and attention drifts.
I have shared the pathway note with the practice lead group so others can adapt it. The thread is being locked now that the case review is complete.
Locking the thread. Thank you everyone — the discussion stays as a reference for the next peer group.

conv-09.content: We are finalising a data sharing agreement across four sites. The sticking point is who owns derived datasets after the project ends.
Our template defers that to the original sites and grants the coordinating centre a licence, not ownership. Reviewers raised no objections.
Licence models need an expiry and a purpose limit or legal will push back. We added both after the first review cycle.
Useful. I will bring both points to the consortium call on Friday and share the revised agreement after.
Following up — we also log every transfer in a register with dates and recipients. Auditors asked for it twice last year and it took minutes to produce.
Adding the register to the draft now. That is the last open item.

replyTo.content: Following up — we also log every transfer in a register with dates and recipients. Auditors asked for it twice last year and it took minutes to produce.

conv-10.content: Updated field safety protocol v3.2 is in the shared folder. Key change: two-person check-in within 30 minutes of any movement in orange zones.
The 30-minute window will be hard in areas with patchy signal. Do we have an offline fallback?
Yes — satellite messenger plus a pre-agreed missed-check-in escalation to the country lead. The annex covers it.
Good. Suggest adding a practice drill to the monthly agenda so the escalation path becomes muscle memory, not a document.
Agreed, adding it. Drills every second month, scenarios rotated.
We ran the first drill — check-in failures were reported fast, but the escalation contact list had two outdated numbers.
Thank you — we will re-verify the roster quarterly and record it as a standing task. Fixing the two numbers today.

conv-11.content: The youth advisory board met for the first time today — eight members aged 15-19. Notes below, feedback welcome.
Great turnout. What was the first thing they pushed back on?
The name. Advisory felt like they would be consulted, not deciding. They want the mandate to include co-design of the next campaign.
That is a fair point and a good upgrade. Let us write the mandate change into the terms of reference before the second meeting.
Also budget for it — co-design takes time and they should be paid for their hours. Volunteer framing undermines the whole point.
Agreed. I will draft the payment policy and bring it to the leadership meeting. Do we need safeguarding review for paid minors?
Our safeguarding lead says yes — payment cannot change consent arrangements, and we will need a parent or guardian acknowledgement.
Terms of reference draft is ready, including the co-design mandate. Sharing it here before it goes to sign-off.
Reading now. First pass looks strong — I will add two lines on review frequency and get it to the board this week.
One more thing — the board asked to review the campaign brief before the agency sees it. I have added that step to the process list.
